content.thinking:
This intervention emphasizes peer review, accountability, and competitors checking each other's work, hitting competence, integrity, and openness fairly directly, plus it implies consensus among experts worldwide. It's more didactic than narrative but mechanistically credible, so I'd estimate a moderately strong trust effect, maybe around +2.2, making it one of the stronger candidate arms.

I'm settling on non-round estimates across the outcome variables: trust_multidimensional around 2.3, trust_post around 1.55, distrust_post around -1.25, with weaker effects on funding_perceptions (~0.55), policy_role_mean (~0.85), and inst_trust_mean (~0.95), since these feel more diluted by the dry expository tone. There's a slight risk that mentioning rejected studies and gatekeeping could read as groupthink to skeptics, but I think the overall effect stays positive.

Rounding out the remaining variables: belief_post around 1.05, concern_mean around 0.65, policy_general around 0.5, policy_specific_mean around 0.42, behavior_mean around 0.28, donation_ams around 0.06, and newsletter_signup at a tiny 0.009.

content.text: {"reasoning_summary":"The peer-review text is a didactic process-transparency message whose core claim — that independent, competing experts scrutinize and often reject research before publication — maps almost directly onto the competence, integrity and openness (accountability, responsiveness to feedback) facets of the multidimensional trust battery, so I expect an above-average but not top-tier proximal effect (~2.3 points, d≈0.10). It lacks narrative vividness, an ideologically congruent messenger, or interactive corrective feedback, which caps it below the strongest source-credibility/consensus-correction arms. The re-asked single trust and belief items are anchored by pre-treatment measurement, so I shrink them (~1.5 and ~1.0); the embedded consensus cue ('experts across the world consistently reach the same conclusions') gives belief a small lift consistent with consensus-messaging meta-analyses (~1–2 points on belief). Distrust is targeted in mirror image but with smaller magnitude given floor/skew (~-1.25). Downstream outcomes (funding, scientist policy role, institutional trust, concern, policy support, intentions) get sub-point effects that decay with distance from the message, and incentivized behaviors move only trivially (a few cents; under one percentage point on sign-up). parsed_output.reasoning_summary: The peer-review text is a didactic process-transparency message whose core claim — that independent, competing experts scrutinize and often reject research before publication — maps almost directly onto the competence, integrity and openness (accountability, responsiveness to feedback) facets of the multidimensional trust battery, so I expect an above-average but not top-tier proximal effect (~2.3 points, d≈0.10). It lacks narrative vividness, an ideologically congruent messenger, or interactive corrective feedback, which caps it below the strongest source-credibility/consensus-correction arms. The re-asked single trust and belief items are anchored by pre-treatment measurement, so I shrink them (~1.5 and ~1.0); the embedded consensus cue ('experts across the world consistently reach the same conclusions') gives belief a small lift consistent with consensus-messaging meta-analyses (~1–2 points on belief). Distrust is targeted in mirror image but with smaller magnitude given floor/skew (~-1.25). Downstream outcomes (funding, scientist policy role, institutional trust, concern, policy support, intentions) get sub-point effects that decay with distance from the message, and incentivized behaviors move only trivially (a few cents; under one percentage point on sign-up). No plausible backfire mechanism dominates, though gatekeeping language ('many studies are rejected') may mute gains among skeptics.
